exercises.title: Abbreviations Used in Code & Architecture
exercises.subtitle: Learn abbreviations used in software architecture and design: DRY, SOLID, YAGNI, KISS, GRASP, TDA, IoC, DI, AOP, CQS - principle abbreviations explained in professional context.

questions.q: A senior developer comments on your PR: 'This violates DRY - you have the same logic in three places.' What does DRY stand for?
options: Do Repeat Yourself
Don't Repeat Yourself
Dry Run Yield
Dynamic Resource Yielding
questions.explanation: DRY stands for Don't Repeat Yourself. It is a principle stating that every piece of knowledge should have a single, unambiguous representation in a system. Duplicate logic increases maintenance cost and the risk of inconsistencies.

questions.q: The tech lead says: 'We should follow SOLID principles when designing these classes.' What does the 'S' in SOLID stand for?
options: Substitution Principle
Single Responsibility Principle
Static Object Linking Invariant Design
Simplified Object Layer in Design
questions.explanation: The S in SOLID stands for Single Responsibility Principle. SOLID is an acronym for five design principles: Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, and Dependency Inversion. Each letter addresses a different aspect of object-oriented design.

questions.q: During planning, your colleague says: 'YAGNI - let's not build that feature until someone actually needs it.' What does YAGNI mean?
options: You Always Get New Issues
You Aren't Gonna Need It
Yield Abstraction Growth Naturally Iterative
Your Architecture Gets Needlessly Inflated
questions.explanation: YAGNI stands for You Aren't Gonna Need It. It is an Extreme Programming principle advising developers not to add functionality until it is necessary, avoiding over-engineering and speculative features.

questions.q: The architect writes in the design doc: 'Keep it simple - KISS applies here.' What is KISS?
options: Keep It Simple, Stupid
Keep Interfaces Small and Structured
Kernel Integration and System Stability
Keep Incremental Steps Slim
questions.explanation: KISS stands for Keep It Simple, Stupid (sometimes 'Keep It Short and Simple'). It is a design principle stating that most systems work best if they are kept simple rather than made complicated. Unnecessary complexity should be avoided.

questions.q: The code review notes: 'Use IoC here - the class should not instantiate its own dependencies.' What does IoC stand for?
options: Interface over Convention
Inversion of Control
Isolated Object Container
Integration of Components
questions.explanation: IoC stands for Inversion of Control. It is a design principle where the control of creating and managing dependencies is transferred from the class itself to an external framework or container. Dependency Injection (DI) is the most common pattern for implementing IoC.

questions.q: git diff --cached You're reviewing a PR and see the reviewer has added a comment: 'This uses an API endpoint for logging. Consider using a centralized logging service like ELK or Splunk - it'll be much easier to manage logs across multiple microservices.' What does 'ELK' stand for in this context?
options: Error Logging Kernel
Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana
Event Logging Key
Extensible Layering Kit
questions.explanation: ELK is a common abbreviation for Elasticsearch, Logstash, and Kibana - the core components of the popular ELK stack for log management. It's frequently used in microservices architectures to centralize logging data from different services into a single, searchable repository. The misconception here is often confusing 'ELK' with other similar acronyms, so it's crucial to understand its specific meaning within the context of infrastructure and DevOps practices.

questions.q: You're in a Slack channel discussing a new feature for an e-commerce platform. A senior developer, Mark, writes: 'Just to clarify, we'll be using CQRS here - Command Query Responsibility Segregation. It's crucial for scalability and performance when dealing with complex queries.' What does CQRS stand for in this context?
options: Continuous Quality Reporting - a system for monitoring code quality during development.
Command Query Responsibility Segregation - a pattern separating read and write operations.
Centralized Queue Routing - a method for managing asynchronous message processing.
Configured Query Storage - the process of optimizing database queries for speed.
questions.explanation: CQRS is a complex architectural pattern. It stands for Command Query Responsibility Segregation, which means separating the operations that *modify* data (commands) from those that *read* data (queries). This separation allows you to optimize each side independently, leading to better scalability and performance, especially in systems with high read/write loads - this is why Mark emphasized it's crucial for a complex e-commerce platform.

questions.q: During a code review of a new microservice, your team lead, Sarah, notes: 'This service needs to be highly testable. We should implement Dependency Injection.' What does DI stand for in this context? A. Data Integration B. Dependency Inversion C. Dependency Injection D. Design Interface
options: Data Integration
Dependency Inversion
Dependency Injection
Design Interface
questions.explanation: DI stands for *Dependency Injection*, a design pattern where an object receives its dependencies from external sources rather than creating them itself. This is crucial for testability and loose coupling, allowing you to easily mock or stub dependencies during testing. Choosing 'Data Integration' or 'Design Interface' would be incorrect as those terms relate to different software concepts. Importantly, DI promotes flexibility and reduces tight coupling between components.

questions.q: You're discussing a new API design with your team. John suggests using 'RESTful' principles. What does REST stand for in this context?
options: Resource Exchange System Toolkit
Representational State Transfer
Reliable Execution Service Technology
Remote Event Server Terminal
questions.explanation: REST stands for Representational State Transfer. It's an architectural style for networked applications that defines a set of constraints to be used when building scalable and resilient systems. It's important to understand this is *not* a specific technology but rather a design philosophy based on HTTP methods. The other options are incorrect acronyms or misrepresentations of the concept.

questions.q: During a standup meeting, David mentions they're using 'MSA' for their new application architecture. What does MSA stand for in this context?
options: Micro Service Architecture
Modular System Approach
Massive State Application
Multi-Server Automation
questions.explanation: MSA stands for Microservice Architecture. This approach breaks down a large application into smaller, independent services that communicate with each other over a network. It's a key pattern in modern cloud-native development and offers benefits like increased scalability, faster development cycles, and improved fault tolerance. The other options represent different architectural styles or approaches.

exercises.title: Agile Abbreviations
exercises.subtitle: 5 exercises - OKRs vs. KPIs, SAFe Program Increments, DORA metrics, the SPACE framework and WIP limits, and meeting vocabulary like AoB and WoW.

questions.q: A quarterly planning doc contrasts "OKRs" with "KPIs." What's the difference between these two goal-tracking abbreviations?
options: OKRs are used only by startups; KPIs are used only by large enterprises
KPIs are set by individual contributors; OKRs are set only by executives
They're interchangeable terms for the same thing

OKR (Objectives and Key Results) is a goal-setting framework pairing a qualitative, ambitious Objective ("Become the fastest checkout in our category") with a small set of measurable Key Results that define success ("reduce checkout time from 45s to 20s"). A KPI (Key Performance Indicator) is a single ongoing metric tracked continuously to monitor the health of a process or business ("monthly active users," "average response time") - OKRs are typically time-boxed and ambition-driven, while KPIs are typically continuous and health-monitoring focused
questions.explanation: OKRs vs. KPIs is a commonly confused pair because both are "goals expressed as numbers," but they serve different purposes and often coexist within the same organisation. OKRs are typically set per quarter (or another fixed cycle), intentionally ambitious (a "good" OKR completion rate is often considered 70%, not 100% - hitting 100% every time may mean the goals weren't ambitious enough), and used to drive focused, time-boxed initiatives. KPIs are ongoing, continuously monitored metrics that indicate whether a system or process is healthy - they don't have a "target quarter," they're tracked indefinitely, and a sudden KPI change (e.g. churn spiking) is itself the signal, rather than the KPI being a stretch goal. A team might use a KPI ("uptime") as an ongoing health metric while also setting an OKR ("reduce P1 incidents by 50% this quarter") as a time-boxed initiative aimed at improving that same underlying area.

questions.q: A Scaled Agile organisation refers to "planning our next PI" during a "PI Planning" event. What does PI stand for in this context, and how does it relate to a normal sprint?
options: PI stands for "Product Increment," referring to a single sprint's deliverable

PI (Program Increment) is a SAFe (Scaled Agile Framework) term for a longer planning cycle - typically 8-12 weeks, composed of several sprints - during which multiple teams align on a shared set of objectives. "PI Planning" is a large, cross-team event where all teams working on a related program plan their upcoming Program Increment together, ensuring dependencies between teams are surfaced and coordinated in advance rather than discovered mid-sprint
PI stands for "Personal Investment," a term unrelated to Agile methodology
PI is simply another word for "sprint," used interchangeably with no distinction
questions.explanation: PI (Program Increment) is specific to SAFe (Scaled Agile Framework) , the most common framework for coordinating Agile practices across many teams (sometimes hundreds of engineers) working on interdependent parts of a larger system. Why PI Planning exists: individual team sprints work well for a single team's own backlog, but when multiple teams' work is interdependent (Team A's API must ship before Team B can build on it), sprint-level planning alone doesn't surface those cross-team dependencies early enough. PI Planning is a dedicated, often in-person, multi-day event where all teams in a program map out their next 8-12 weeks together, explicitly identifying and negotiating dependencies before the increment begins. This is a good example of vocabulary that only makes sense once you understand the organisational scale it addresses - a single small team would never need "PI Planning," since coordination overhead at that scale would outweigh the benefit; it becomes valuable specifically when many teams' work is tightly coupled.

questions.q: A DevOps team reviews their "DORA metrics" in a quarterly retrospective. What does DORA stand for, and what category of metrics does it refer to?
options: DORA stands for "Daily Operations Review Agenda" - a meeting format, not a metrics framework
DORA stands for "Data Operations Reporting Automation" - a data pipeline monitoring tool

DORA refers to the DevOps Research and Assessment team/research programme, whose research identified four key metrics correlated with high-performing engineering teams: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and time to restore service. "DORA metrics" has become shorthand for tracking these four specific software delivery performance indicators
DORA is an acronym for a specific CI/CD tool, similar to Jenkins or GitHub Actions
questions.explanation: DORA (from the DevOps Research and Assessment group, whose work is summarised in the well-known "Accelerate" book and the annual State of DevOps Report) established four metrics as empirically correlated with software delivery performance and, ultimately, organisational outcomes: • Deployment frequency - how often code is deployed to production • Lead time for changes - how long from code committed to code running in production • Change failure rate - what percentage of deployments cause a failure requiring remediation • Time to restore service - how quickly the team recovers from a production incident "DORA metrics" is now standard vocabulary in engineering leadership and platform engineering conversations for benchmarking delivery performance objectively, rather than relying on anecdote or gut feeling about "how fast are we shipping."

questions.q: An engineering culture document references "the SPACE framework" for measuring developer productivity, contrasted with just tracking "WIP limits." How do these two concepts relate?
options: WIP limits are a subset of KPIs, unrelated to SPACE

SPACE (Satisfaction and well-being, Performance, Activity, Communication and collaboration, Efficiency and flow) is a holistic framework arguing that developer productivity can't be captured by a single metric (like raw commit count), and should be assessed across these five dimensions instead. WIP (Work In Progress) limits are a specific, narrower practice - capping how many tasks a team or individual is actively working on at once, based on the observation that excessive multitasking reduces overall throughput and flow - one small tactic that could improve the "Efficiency and flow" dimension of SPACE, not a competing framework
SPACE is a project management tool, while WIP is a metric it produces
They measure exactly the same thing and are redundant to use together
questions.explanation: Understanding how a broad framework (SPACE) relates to a specific tactical practice (WIP limits) it can encompass is a useful skill for engineering-culture conversations, since these terms are often mentioned together without the relationship being made explicit. SPACE was proposed specifically as a corrective to the common mistake of measuring developer productivity with a single, easily-gamed metric like lines of code or commit count. It argues productivity should be assessed across five distinct dimensions, since optimising for only one (e.g. Activity) can actively harm others (e.g. Satisfaction, if it drives burnout). WIP (Work In Progress) limits , borrowed from Kanban and lean manufacturing, cap how many items can be "in progress" simultaneously on a board, forcing a team to finish existing work before starting new work - this directly targets flow efficiency (less context-switching, faster individual task completion), one concrete lever within SPACE's "Efficiency and flow" dimension rather than a standalone competing philosophy.

questions.q: A retrospective facilitator writes on the board: "AoB" at the end of the agenda, alongside a note about the team's "WoW." What do these two abbreviations mean in this context?
options: AoB and WoW are both formal SAFe ceremonies with fixed, mandatory agendas
AoB stands for "Agile or Bust," a slogan; WoW stands for a specific software tool
Both are typos with no real meaning

AoB (Any Other Business) is a standard meeting-agenda item - a catch-all slot at the end for topics that weren't on the formal agenda but a participant wants to raise briefly. WoW (Ways of Working) refers to a team's agreed-upon practices and norms - how they run standups, how they handle code review, how they define "done" - often revisited explicitly during retrospectives to decide what to keep or change
questions.explanation: AoB (Any Other Business) is common meeting-agenda vocabulary (not exclusive to Agile) - a deliberate, bounded slot at the end of an agenda for unplanned but relevant topics, preventing meetings from either running long chasing tangents mid-discussion or leaving legitimate concerns unraised entirely. WoW (Ways of Working) is genuinely Agile/team-culture-specific vocabulary - it refers to the collective, often informally-agreed set of practices a team follows: their Definition of Done, their branching strategy, how strictly they follow sprint ceremonies, their code review SLA, and similar operational norms. Retrospectives frequently include an explicit "should we change our WoW?" discussion, distinct from simply discussing what went well/poorly in the last sprint - it's specifically about the team's own process rules, which are expected to evolve over time as the team learns what works for them. Both abbreviations are common in meeting notes and retrospective templates, and recognising them quickly avoids the awkwardness of asking "wait, what does that mean?" mid-meeting.

questions.q: PR was added to the backlog during sprint planning. The team lead asks you, 'Can you please update the PR description with more detail about the changes and their impact?' Which of the following best describes what PR means in this context?
options: Performance Review - an assessment of an individual developer's work performance.
Project Report - a document summarizing the progress and outcomes of a specific project.
Product Release - the official launch of a new version of the software.
Pull Request - a request to merge code changes into a main branch.
questions.explanation: PR (Pull Request) is a core concept in Agile development, specifically within Git workflows. It represents a proposed change to the codebase that needs review and approval before being integrated. The other options - Product Release, Performance Review, and Project Report - all have distinct meanings unrelated to this specific scenario; understanding PR as a request for code review is crucial for effective collaboration.

questions.q: During a Slack discussion about the upcoming feature release, Sarah says, 'We need to ensure this API endpoint adheres to the RESTful principles. Let's make sure our documentation is up-to-date and we're consistently using verbs in the HTTP methods - GET, POST, PUT, DELETE.' Which of the following best describes what 'REST' means in this context?
options: c. Real-time System Testing - a testing technique focused on immediate feedback.
d. Resource-Oriented Software Technology - a framework for building scalable web services.
a. Rapid Application Development - a software development methodology.
b. Representational State Transfer - an architectural style for networked applications.
questions.explanation: REST stands for Representational State Transfer and is an architectural style used to design networked applications. It's not about rapid development or any specific technology; instead, it defines how clients and servers should interact using standard protocols like HTTP. Using verbs like GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE correctly aligns with the core principles of RESTful API design, ensuring predictable and standardized interactions.

questions.q: Liam : "Hey team, I've just received this API response from the new authentication service. It's returning a 401 Unauthorized error for users who haven't completed their profile information. Should we prioritize addressing this in our next sprint?" Which of the following best explains what '401' means in this context, based on typical REST API responses?
options: Authorization failure - the user needs to log in.
Server overload - the server is temporarily unable to handle requests.
Data validation error - the request body does not conform to expected schema.
Request timeout - the server did not respond within the allotted time.
questions.explanation: A 401 Unauthorized status code signifies that the client (in this case, the API calling the authentication service) must provide valid credentials before proceeding. It's a standard HTTP response indicating an incorrect authentication attempt; options B, C, and D represent other error codes or conditions unrelated to authentication issues. Understanding these codes is crucial for debugging and troubleshooting API interactions.

questions.q: David : 'Okay team, I've just pushed this PR with the new user onboarding flow. The description mentions 'TDD', but I'm not sure everyone fully understands what that means in our context. Can someone briefly explain it to me before we move on?' Which of the following best describes what 'TDD' stands for within a typical software development team's PR and code review process?
options: Technical Design Document - a formal document outlining system architecture.
Team Dependency Diagram - a visual representation of how teams collaborate on projects.
Task Definition Directive - a set of instructions for completing assigned tasks efficiently.
Test-Driven Development - a coding practice where tests are written before the code itself.
questions.explanation: 'TDD' stands for Test-Driven Development. It's a core agile practice where developers write automated tests before writing the actual code to implement a feature. This ensures that the code meets the requirements and helps catch bugs early on. Misunderstanding TDD can lead to issues with testing coverage, so it's important to ensure everyone understands this key agile principle.

questions.q: During a code review session, Mark comments on a pull request: 'This change introduces significant technical debt. We should refactor this section to improve readability and maintainability.' He then asks you to add a comment to the PR description referencing the need for 'Boy Scout Rule' . What does the 'Boy Scout Rule' refer to in this context?
options: 'Always leave the campground cleaner than you found it' - a general principle of leaving code better than you received it, emphasizing quality and improvement.
A specific coding standard requiring all code comments to be written in uppercase for clarity.
An Agile methodology that prioritizes minimizing the codebase size at all costs.
The practice of adding unnecessary complexity to solve a problem, ultimately making future development more difficult.
questions.explanation: The 'Boy Scout Rule' is a common idiom in software development that emphasizes taking on extra tasks to improve things beyond the immediate requirements. Mark's comment highlights a need for refactoring and leaving the code base better than it was before - this aligns perfectly with the spirit of the Boy Scout Rule. The other options describe specific coding practices or methodologies, but don't capture the core meaning of proactively adding value.

exercises.title: Cloud Abbreviations
exercises.subtitle: 5 exercises - IaaS/PaaS/SaaS/FaaS/CaaS service models, SLA vs. SLO vs. SLI, CDN edge caching, and spot instance tradeoffs.

questions.q: A vendor comparison table lists "IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS" as three cloud service models. What do these three abbreviations mean, and how do they differ?
options: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) provides raw compute, storage, and networking, and you manage the OS and everything above it (e.g. AWS EC2). PaaS (Platform as a Service) additionally manages the OS and runtime, so you just deploy code (e.g. Heroku, Azure App Service). SaaS (Software as a Service) is a complete, ready-to-use application, and you manage nothing but your data and configuration (e.g. Salesforce, Gmail)
IaaS is for individuals, PaaS is for partnerships, SaaS is for enterprises
IaaS runs on-premises, PaaS runs in a private cloud, SaaS runs in a public cloud - the distinction is purely about location
They're three different names for the same thing - the marketing term varies by vendor
questions.explanation: IaaS / PaaS / SaaS describe an increasing level of abstraction, and correspondingly, decreasing responsibility for the customer. The standard way to remember it: as you move from IaaS to SaaS, you manage less and the provider manages more. Each layer builds on the one below it - a SaaS product is typically built on top of PaaS or IaaS infrastructure that the vendor manages internally. These abbreviations are foundational vocabulary for describing any cloud architecture decision - "should we run this ourselves on IaaS, or use a managed PaaS" is one of the most common early architecture conversations in any project.

questions.q: A newer term appears in a serverless architecture discussion: "FaaS" and "CaaS". How do these relate to the more familiar IaaS/PaaS/SaaS model?
options: FaaS (Function as a Service) lets you deploy individual functions that run on-demand without managing any server at all (e.g. AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions) - an even more abstracted model than PaaS. CaaS (Container as a Service) is a managed platform specifically for running containers, sitting between IaaS and PaaS in abstraction (e.g. AWS ECS/Fargate, Google Cloud Run)
FaaS stands for "Firewall as a Service" and CaaS for "Compliance as a Service"
FaaS and CaaS are unrelated marketing terms with no technical meaning
FaaS and CaaS are only used by AWS, no other cloud provider has equivalents
questions.explanation: FaaS (Function as a Service) is the technical foundation of "serverless" computing - you write a single function, it runs only when triggered (an HTTP request, a queue message, a scheduled event), scales automatically, and you're billed per invocation/execution time rather than for an always-running server. CaaS (Container as a Service) gives you the flexibility of packaging your app as a container (more control than FaaS, since you're not limited to a single function's execution model) without managing the underlying servers or orchestration cluster yourself. Recognising the full family - IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, FaaS, CaaS - and correctly slotting a new product announcement into the right category ("is this FaaS or PaaS?") is a common technical vocabulary test in architecture discussions and cloud certification exams alike.

questions.q: A support ticket references "our SLA guarantees 99.95% uptime." What does SLA stand for, and how does this relate to the terms "SLO" and "SLI" that often appear alongside it?
options: SLA, SLO, and SLI are three interchangeable acronyms for the exact same concept
SLA stands for "Server Load Average" and describes hardware capacity
SLI is a legal document and SLA is just an internal team target - the reverse of the correct relationship

SLA (Service Level Agreement) is a legally-binding external commitment to a customer, often with financial penalties for breach; an SLO (Service Level Objective) is the internal target a team sets for itself (often stricter than the SLA, to leave margin); an SLI (Service Level Indicator) is the actual measured metric (e.g. real uptime percentage) used to evaluate whether the SLO/SLA is being met
questions.explanation: SLA / SLO / SLI form a related trio that's frequently tested and frequently confused. The relationship, from most to least formal: • SLA (Service Level Agreement) - an external, often contractual commitment made to customers, typically with defined consequences (service credits, refunds) if breached • SLO (Service Level Objective) - an internal target the engineering team holds itself to, usually set stricter than the SLA to provide a safety margin before actually breaching the customer-facing commitment • SLI (Service Level Indicator) - the actual, concrete measurement (e.g. "percentage of requests completed under 200ms," "percentage of successful requests") used to determine whether the SLO/SLA is currently being met Memory aid: Agreement (external, legal) → Objective (internal, target) → Indicator (measured, real number) - moving from the most formal/external to the most concrete/measurable.

questions.q: A content delivery discussion mentions "using a CDN to reduce latency for users in different regions." What does CDN stand for, and why does it reduce latency specifically?
options: Cloud Domain Name - a naming convention for cloud resources
Continuous Deployment Network - a network used specifically for CI/CD pipelines
Central Data Node - a single powerful server that handles all requests from one location

Content Delivery Network - a geographically distributed network of servers that caches and serves content from a location physically closer to the requesting user, reducing the network distance (and therefore latency) data has to travel compared to serving every request from one central origin server
questions.explanation: CDN (Content Delivery Network) works by caching content (static files, images, sometimes API responses) at many "edge" locations around the world. When a user requests content, it's served from the nearest edge server rather than travelling all the way to a single origin server, which directly reduces round-trip network latency - the physical distance data has to travel is often the dominant factor in perceived load time for geographically distant users. Related vocabulary commonly paired with CDN: edge location (a CDN's regional server), cache hit/miss (whether content was already cached at that edge location or had to be fetched from origin), origin server (the source server the CDN pulls from when content isn't cached), TTL (Time To Live) (how long cached content is considered valid before the CDN re-fetches it from origin).

questions.q: A cloud cost-optimisation discussion mentions "moving to spot instances could reduce our EC2 costs" alongside "we should check our SLA before switching." How would you explain the tradeoff being discussed?
options: Spot instances are a security feature unrelated to cost
SLA and spot instances are unrelated concepts mentioned together by coincidence
Spot instances have no tradeoff - they're always strictly better than regular instances

Spot instances (spare cloud capacity offered at a steep discount) can be reclaimed by the provider with little notice when demand rises elsewhere, so they're much cheaper but less reliable - appropriate for fault-tolerant or interruptible workloads (batch jobs, non-critical background processing), but risky for services with strict uptime commitments (an SLA), since an interrupted spot instance could cause an SLA breach
questions.explanation: This scenario tests whether you can connect two separate abbreviations (spot instances aren't technically an abbreviation, but the cost-vs-reliability tradeoff vocabulary and the SLA concept) into a coherent architecture decision - a common real-world pattern in cloud cost conversations. Spot instances (AWS terminology; other clouds use similar concepts like "preemptible VMs" on GCP) offer significant discounts (often 60-90% off on-demand pricing) in exchange for the provider's right to reclaim the capacity with short notice when it's needed elsewhere. Why the SLA connection matters: if a workload is running under a customer-facing SLA promising high availability, running it entirely on interruptible spot instances without a fallback strategy risks breaching that SLA when instances are reclaimed. The mature approach - often described as a mixed fleet - runs a baseline of on-demand (or reserved) instances to guarantee SLA-covered capacity, supplemented by spot instances for the elastic, interruption-tolerant portion of the workload.

options: Open Identity Data Carrier
Object-Oriented Development Cycle
Operational Information Delivery Channel
Online Identity Definition Component
questions.explanation: OIDC (OpenID Connect) is a standard authentication protocol built on top of OAuth 2.0. It's frequently used for single sign-on and federated identity management - in this case, Mark is referring to using OIDC to securely authenticate users via Auth0. questions.q: PR #5678 is titled 'Deploy: Migrate Database to RDS'. During a standup update, David says, 'We're using Lambda functions to orchestrate the data migration. We've configured DynamoDB Streams for change capture and then triggered a Lambda function on every change.' What does DynamoDB Streams primarily facilitate in this scenario?
options: Data encryption at rest - ensuring sensitive information is protected.
Automated backups of the RDS database instance, providing disaster recovery capabilities.
Real-time synchronization between two database instances, offering immediate updates across systems.
Event-driven architecture - reacting to changes in data sources and triggering automated actions based on those changes.
questions.explanation: DynamoDB Streams is a key component of AWS's event-driven architecture. It allows you to capture changes made to DynamoDB tables in real-time and then react to those changes by triggering other services, like Lambda functions, as David describes. options: Data encryption of files stored in S3.
Securely managing access permissions for AWS resources, like Lambda and S3.
Automatic scaling of the API Gateway based on request volume.
Monitoring the performance of the Lambda function executions.
questions.explanation: IAM (Identity and Access Management) is crucial for controlling who or what can access other AWS services. In this scenario, the IAM role grants the Lambda function the necessary permissions to read from and write to S3, ensuring only authorized actions are performed - preventing unauthorized data access. Options A, C, and D represent related functionalities but don't directly address the core purpose of IAM as a permission management system.

questions.q: PR #7890 is titled 'Implement Monitoring with CloudWatch'. During a technical discussion, Emily says, 'We need to set up alarms based on CPU utilization and error rates. We'll use CloudWatch Metrics for this.' Mark replies, 'Sounds good - we should also consider using CloudWatch Logs Insights to analyze our log data.' What does CloudWatch primarily facilitate in this scenario?
options: A: Direct access to the underlying hardware of our servers.
D: Real-time communication between different microservices within the application.
C: Secure storage for sensitive data, ensuring compliance with GDPR regulations.
B: Automated scaling based on pre-defined thresholds, alongside log analysis and metric monitoring.
questions.explanation: CloudWatch is a comprehensive monitoring service. It's core functionality involves collecting and tracking metrics (like CPU utilization) and logs from various AWS resources, allowing for automated scaling and alerting based on defined thresholds-as Emily describes. While CloudWatch Logs Insights *does* analyze log data, the primary purpose of CloudWatch in this scenario is broader monitoring, not just log analysis. Option A is incorrect as CloudWatch doesn't provide direct hardware access.

questions.q: During a Slack discussion about migrating to Kubernetes on AWS, Alex writes: 'We're going with EKS - it seems like the best way to manage our containers.' Ben replies: 'Good call! We'll also be using ECS for some of our legacy applications.' What is the primary difference between EKS and ECS in this context?
options: EKS is a fully managed database service, while ECS manages container orchestration. insufficient - the account balance is too low...
Both EKS and ECS are identical services; the choice depends solely on personal preference.
EKS is a serverless computing platform, whereas ECS manages traditional virtual machines.
ECS is a managed Kubernetes service, providing a simpler way to deploy and manage containerized applications without the operational overhead of managing a full Kubernetes cluster.
questions.explanation: EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service) and ECS (Elastic Container Service) are both container orchestration services offered by AWS, but they differ significantly in their complexity. EKS is a managed version of Kubernetes, offering the full power and flexibility of Kubernetes with reduced operational burden, while ECS is a simpler service focused on deploying and managing containers within an AWS environment. The key difference lies in the level of control and management required - EKS provides more granular control through Kubernetes primitives.

questions.q: GKE, AKS, and EKS are all managed Kubernetes services. Which clouds do they belong to?
options: GKE = Azure, AKS = AWS, EKS = Google
GKE = Google Cloud, AKS = Azure, EKS = AWS
GKE = AWS, AKS = Google, EKS = Azure
They are all AWS services
questions.explanation: GKE (Google Kubernetes Engine) is Google Cloud's managed Kubernetes. AKS (Azure Kubernetes Service) is Microsoft Azure's offering. EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service) is AWS's. All three manage the Kubernetes control plane so you only manage worker nodes.

questions.q: What does IAM stand for and what is its function in cloud platforms?
options: Internet Access Manager - manages internet connections
Identity and Access Management - controls who can do what to which cloud resources
Infrastructure Automation Module - automates infrastructure provisioning
Integrated Application Manager - manages cloud applications
questions.explanation: IAM (Identity and Access Management) is the system that controls authentication and authorization in cloud platforms. IAM policies define which users, roles, or services can perform which actions on which resources.

questions.q: What is the difference between TLS and mTLS?
options: TLS is older, mTLS is newer
TLS (Transport Layer Security) authenticates the server to the client; mTLS (mutual TLS) additionally authenticates the client to the server - both parties verify each other's identity
TLS is for web traffic, mTLS is for databases
TLS encrypts data, mTLS compresses data
questions.explanation: Standard TLS lets the client verify the server's identity (via certificate). mTLS (mutual TLS) requires both sides to present certificates - the server also verifies the client. mTLS is widely used in zero-trust service mesh architectures (e.g., Istio).

questions.q: What does CIDR stand for and what does a notation like '10.0.0.0/16' mean?
options: Cloud Infrastructure Design Reference
Classless Inter-Domain Routing - a notation for IP address ranges where /16 means the first 16 bits are the network address, giving 65,536 possible addresses
Configured IP and DNS Routing - a DNS configuration format
Container IP Distribution Registry - a way to assign IPs to containers
questions.explanation: CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) notation describes IP address ranges. '10.0.0.0/16' means the first 16 bits are fixed (10.0.x.x), giving 65,536 addresses. VPC and subnet sizes are always expressed in CIDR notation.

questions.q: What is the difference between OAuth 2.0 and OIDC?
options: They are the same protocol
OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework (what you can do); OIDC (OpenID Connect) adds an authentication layer on top (who you are) - OIDC is built on OAuth 2.0
OAuth is for mobile apps, OIDC is for web apps
OIDC is older and OAuth 2.0 replaced it
questions.explanation: OAuth 2.0 handles authorization - delegating access to resources without sharing passwords. OIDC (OpenID Connect) is a thin identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that adds authentication - an ID token that tells you who the user is. Most SSO implementations use OIDC.

exercises.title: Data Abbreviations
exercises.subtitle: 5 exercises - ETL vs. ELT, OLTP vs. OLAP, Change Data Capture (CDC), RPO vs. RTO disaster recovery targets, and connecting data vocabulary in real scenarios.

questions.q: A data engineer explains: "We're rebuilding our ETL pipeline as ELT instead." What's the difference between ETL and ELT?
options: ETL runs continuously; ELT only runs once per day
They're the same process; ELT is just a newer marketing term for ETL

ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) transforms data before loading it into the destination warehouse - transformation happens in a separate processing step. ELT (Extract, Load, Transform) loads raw data into the destination first, then transforms it there, using the destination's own processing power (common with modern cloud data warehouses like Snowflake or BigQuery that can handle large-scale transformation efficiently)
ETL is used only for structured data; ELT is used only for unstructured data
questions.explanation: The ETL-to-ELT shift reflects how modern cloud data warehouses (a DWH , or data warehouse) became powerful enough to handle transformation workloads themselves, removing the need for a separate transformation server/step before loading. ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) - the traditional pattern: pull data from a source, transform/clean/reshape it in a dedicated processing layer, then load the finished result into the warehouse. This front-loads all transformation logic before data ever lands in the warehouse. ELT (Extract, Load, Transform) - load raw data into the warehouse first, then run transformations as SQL (or dbt models) directly against the warehouse's compute. This is now the dominant pattern for cloud-native data stacks, since it keeps raw data available for re-processing and leverages the warehouse's scalable compute rather than a separate ETL server.

questions.q: A database architecture discussion contrasts "OLTP" and "OLAP" systems. What's the fundamental difference, and why can't one database type efficiently serve both purposes?
options: OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) is optimised for many small, fast read/write operations - the typical pattern of an application database handling individual orders, logins, or updates. OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) is optimised for complex queries scanning and aggregating large volumes of historical data - the typical pattern of analytics and reporting. Their storage and indexing strategies conflict: OLTP favours row-based storage for fast single-record access, while OLAP favours column-based storage for fast aggregation across many records, which is why the two workloads are usually separated into different systems
OLTP and OLAP are simply different names for SQL and NoSQL databases
OLAP databases don't support SQL, only OLTP databases do
OLTP is for internal company data; OLAP is for customer-facing data
questions.explanation: The OLTP vs. OLAP distinction explains why companies typically run a separate analytics/reporting database (data warehouse) rather than running heavy analytical queries directly against their production application database. OLTP - designed for high-concurrency, low-latency operations on individual records (insert an order, update a user's profile). Uses row-based storage, since a full row is usually read/written together. Running a large analytical query (e.g. "total revenue by region for the last 3 years") against an OLTP database can be slow and, worse, can lock rows or consume resources needed for live application traffic. OLAP - designed for scanning and aggregating large volumes of data efficiently. Uses column-based storage, since analytical queries typically read a few columns across many rows (e.g. just amount and region , summed across millions of rows) rather than entire rows. This is precisely why CDC (Change Data Capture) - streaming changes from the OLTP database into an OLAP warehouse - exists as a standard pattern: it keeps analytics fresh without burdening the production database.

questions.q: A database replication discussion mentions "using CDC to stream changes from Postgres into our data warehouse in near real-time." What does CDC stand for, and how does it differ from a nightly batch export?
options: Change Data Capture - a technique that captures and streams individual row-level changes (inserts, updates, deletes) from a source database as they happen, typically by reading the database's transaction log, rather than periodically re-exporting the entire dataset in a batch job. This means downstream systems (like a data warehouse) receive near real-time updates rather than data that's up to 24 hours stale after a nightly batch job
Central Data Cluster - a term for a database's primary server
Cloud Data Connector - a generic term for any API integration between two cloud services
Compressed Data Chunk - a data storage format optimised for network transfer
questions.explanation: CDC (Change Data Capture) is a foundational technique in modern data pipelines, enabling near-real-time data synchronisation without the overhead of repeatedly scanning and re-exporting an entire source table. How it typically works: CDC tools (e.g. Debezium, or built-in features of some cloud databases) read the source database's transaction log (also called the write-ahead log or binlog, depending on the database) - the internal record every database already maintains of every change - and stream those changes to a downstream consumer (a message queue, then a data warehouse) as they occur. Why this beats a nightly batch export: a full nightly export means downstream analytics are always up to 24 hours stale, and re-exporting an entire large table repeatedly wastes resources on data that hasn't changed. CDC only propagates what actually changed, arriving with much lower latency - often seconds to minutes rather than a full day.

questions.q: A disaster recovery plan states: "Our RPO is 15 minutes and our RTO is 2 hours." How would you explain these two targets to a non-technical stakeholder?
options: RPO and RTO are legal terms with no technical meaning, used only in contracts
RPO refers to the recovery team's staffing plan; RTO refers to the backup storage cost

RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is how much data loss is acceptable, measured in time - "15 minutes" means, in a disaster, you might lose up to the last 15 minutes of data since the last backup/replication point. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is how long it's acceptable for the system to be unavailable before it's restored - "2 hours" means the team commits to having the system back up within 2 hours of a disaster being declared
They both mean the same thing - how long the system can be down
questions.explanation: RPO and RTO are the two core metrics of any disaster recovery plan, and precisely distinguishing them is essential since they drive very different engineering investments. RPO (Recovery Point Objective) answers "how much data can we afford to lose?" - it's driven by how frequently data is backed up or replicated. A tighter RPO (e.g. near-zero) requires continuous replication to a standby system; a looser RPO (e.g. 24 hours) can be satisfied by nightly backups alone. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) answers "how long can we afford to be down?" - it's driven by how quickly a failover or restoration process can complete. A tight RTO (minutes) typically requires an already-running standby system ready to take over instantly (hot standby); a looser RTO (hours/days) might allow restoring from backups onto freshly provisioned infrastructure. Explaining a DR plan clearly to stakeholders means stating both numbers together - "we could lose up to 15 minutes of data, and we'd be back online within 2 hours" - since either number alone tells only half the story.

questions.q: A data platform review notes: "Our OLTP database's SLA guarantees 99.9% availability, but our nightly ETL job occasionally causes replication lag that briefly affects our OLAP dashboards." How would you summarise this situation using the correct terms?
options: "OLAP and OLTP are the same database, so an issue in one is automatically an issue in both."

"Our production (OLTP) database itself remains highly available per its SLA - the issue is specifically that our ETL pipeline periodically introduces replication lag, meaning our analytical (OLAP) dashboards show slightly stale data during and shortly after the nightly load, not that the production system is down."
"The SLA covers both the OLTP database and the OLAP dashboards equally, so this is a contractual breach."
"The dashboards being briefly out of date has nothing to do with the ETL job."
questions.explanation: This scenario tests whether you can correctly connect multiple data-engineering abbreviations into one precise, accurate technical summary - a genuinely valuable communication skill when reporting incidents or explaining architecture to stakeholders who might otherwise conflate "the database is down" with "the dashboard shows old data," which are very different severities. Precise summary components: • The SLA applies specifically to the production OLTP system - its own separate availability commitment, unaffected by the ETL job • Replication lag - the delay between a change happening in the source and that change being reflected downstream - is the specific mechanism causing staleness, distinct from an outage • The OLAP dashboards being briefly stale is a data-freshness issue, not an availability issue, and typically doesn't violate any uptime SLA at all (unless a separate freshness SLA exists for the dashboards specifically) Being able to say precisely "this is a data-freshness issue in the OLAP layer, not an availability issue in the OLTP layer" prevents an overreaction (treating a minor lag as a major outage) and correctly directs the fix toward the ETL/replication pipeline rather than the production database.

a potential indicator of a data quality problem, specifically concerning incorrect data serialization formats being produced by the upstream producer.
insufficient - the consumer is simply processing slower under heavy load.
a minor issue related to Kafka's inherent performance characteristics, easily resolved with increased cluster resources.
questions.explanation: This PR description highlights a situation where schema evolution in Kafka is likely the root cause. options: acceptable - 80ms spike during peak hours is within industry standards for a GraphQL endpoint.
informative but doesn't highlight potential issues; further monitoring is needed.
insufficient - the API response time is acceptable for most users.
critical - immediate investigation required due to high latency impacting user experience.
questions.explanation: The primary concern here isn't just the average latency (20ms), which might be acceptable. The description explicitly states 'occasional spikes to 80ms,' and this sudden increase during peak hours is what demands immediate attention. High latency during critical times can significantly degrade user experience, making it a 'critical' issue for investigation and remediation - option 1 correctly identifies this.

questions.q: Reviewer: "I noticed you're using the term 'CQRS' here. Can you explain why we're separating read and write models? It seems complex."
options: CQRS is an acronym for 'Consistent Query Result Set,' representing a technique where all queries return the same result regardless of the underlying data changes.
CQRS stands for 'Central Query Routing System,' a method of optimizing database queries by directing them to specific servers based on their data content.
CQRS refers to a specific database technology, like CockroachDB, which natively supports this pattern. It's not just a concept; it's a product.

CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) is an architectural pattern that separates the logic for handling commands (write operations) from the logic for handling queries (read operations). This separation improves scalability and performance by allowing different models optimized for each function.
questions.explanation: The core idea behind CQRS isn't just about routing queries; it's a design pattern. CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) separates how you handle writing data (commands) from how you retrieve data (queries). This allows for optimization - a read model can be designed specifically for fast, efficient querying without needing to worry about the complexities of write operations, and vice versa. It's a powerful technique for scaling applications with varying read and write loads.

questions.q: Reviewer: 'I'm seeing a lot of discussion about 'schemas' in the data warehouse. Can you clarify what a schema is and why we're using different ones for our staging area versus our production tables? It seems like it should just be one big table.'

B: A schema defines the structure of a database - its tables, columns, and relationships - and we're using separate schemas for staging (raw incoming data) and production (transformed, validated data) to manage data quality and evolution.

questions.explanation: The correct answer highlights the fundamental definition of a database schema as defining the structure of a database. The other options misinterpret 'schema' - it's not just a database name or solely related to user permissions or physical storage. Using separate schemas for staging and production is a common practice in data warehousing to manage different stages of data transformation and maintain data integrity.

exercises.title: DevOps & SRE Abbreviations
exercises.subtitle: Practice common DevOps and SRE abbreviations: SLO, SLI, SLA, MTTR, MTTD, DORA, CI/CD, IaC, GitOps, FinOps, and incident management terms.

questions.q: What is the difference between an SLI, SLO, and SLA?
options: They are all the same thing
SLI (Service Level Indicator) is the metric measured; SLO (Service Level Objective) is the target; SLA (Service Level Agreement) is the contractual commitment with penalties
SLI is for internal teams, SLO is for customers, SLA is for regulators
SLA is the metric, SLO is the contract, SLI is the alert
questions.explanation: SLI is the actual measurement (e.g., 99.7% uptime this month). SLO is the internal target (e.g., 99.9% uptime). SLA is the contractual agreement with customers (e.g., 99.5% uptime or we pay credits). SLOs should be stricter than SLAs.

questions.q: What does MTTR stand for and why is it important?
options: Mean Time To Release - how long releases take
Mean Time To Recovery - how long it takes to restore service after an incident
Mean Time To Review - code review speed
Mean Time To Response - how fast support replies
questions.explanation: MTTR (Mean Time To Recovery) measures how quickly your team can restore service after a failure. It's one of the four DORA metrics. A low MTTR indicates mature incident response processes and good observability.

questions.q: What does 'IaC' stand for and what problem does it solve?
options: Internet as a Computer
Infrastructure as Code - managing infrastructure through code and version control instead of manual configuration
Internal as Configuration
Infrastructure as a Container
questions.explanation: IaC (Infrastructure as Code) means your servers, networks, and cloud resources are defined in code files (Terraform, Pulumi, CloudFormation). This enables version control, repeatability, and eliminates 'works on my cloud' problems.

questions.q: What does 'GitOps' mean in a DevOps context?
options: Using Git to store documentation
A practice where Git repositories are the single source of truth for infrastructure and deployment state - changes are made via Git commits, not manual commands
A Git branching strategy
A way to organize Git repositories
questions.explanation: GitOps means your Git repository is the source of truth. When you want to change infrastructure or deploy code, you commit to Git - automated systems (like Flux or ArgoCD) detect the change and reconcile the actual state to match.

questions.q: In PagerDuty incident management, what do ACK, SNOOZE, and RESOLVE mean?
options: Account Keys, Service Notes, Routing Verification
ACK (Acknowledge) - I'm aware of the incident; SNOOZE - temporarily suppress alerts; RESOLVE - the incident is fixed
All Create Knowledge, Store New Operations, Report Event
Alert Confirm, Stop Notification, Reset Event
questions.explanation: In PagerDuty: ACK (Acknowledge) means you're aware and working on it; SNOOZE temporarily silences alerts for a set period (useful during maintenance); RESOLVE closes the incident and stops all alerts. These are standard on-call response actions.

questions.q: During a code review for the new microservice deployment, Sarah from SRE sends this message to the team channel: 'We're seeing an increase in 5xx errors - let's investigate. The *E2E latency* is spiking and hitting 300ms, which is significantly above our SLO of 150ms.' Which of the following best describes what Sarah is referring to?
options: A. A temporary network outage affecting all services.
B. The time it takes for a request to travel from the user's browser to the database and back, including processing time.
C. The total time spent by developers fixing bugs in the code.
D. The number of times an HTTP request fails due to server errors.
questions.explanation: E2E latency (End-to-End Latency) specifically measures the duration of a request as it traverses the entire system - from user input to database response. Sarah is highlighting a performance issue that's exceeding their Service Level Objective (SLO), which focuses on availability and responsiveness. While 5xx errors are problematic, E2E latency provides context about *where* the problem originates, differentiating it from simply counting error rates.

questions.q: During a Slack discussion about the recent performance issues with the new user authentication service, David (a Developer) posted: 'Just ran some tests and the API response time is consistently above 800ms. We're hitting our 500ms SLO!'. Maria from SRE replied: 'That's concerning - let's examine the TTFB .' Which of the following best explains what Maria meant in this context?
options: The total number of requests processed by the authentication service.
The time taken for the initial HTTP request to reach the server (from the client's perspective).
The amount of data transferred during the API call.
The duration of the processing performed by the application code on the server.
questions.explanation: TTFB stands for 'Time To First Byte'. It's a crucial metric in performance monitoring and represents the delay between sending an HTTP request and receiving the first byte of data from the server. Developers often focus on overall response times, but understanding TTFB helps pinpoint bottlenecks within the network or server-side processing. The other options represent different aspects of API calls (request volume, data transfer, or server-side processing time) rather than the initial delay.

questions.q: During a standup update, Ben (DevOps Engineer) says: 'We're seeing some intermittent issues with the order processing service - specifically, we've observed occasional timeouts when submitting orders during peak hours. Our 99% availability SLA is being impacted.' He then mentions the team is investigating potential bottlenecks in the database query performance. Which of the following terms best describes the *underlying cause* Ben is likely referring to?
options: Operational Excellence - focusing on efficiency and minimizing disruption.
Chaos Engineering - deliberately introducing failures to test resilience.
Database Bottleneck - a limitation in the database's capacity or performance that's causing delays.
Service Level Agreement - a formal contract defining expected service availability.
questions.explanation: Ben is using 'database bottleneck' to describe the issue. While an SLA (option 4) outlines *what* is being measured and the target performance, a database bottleneck refers to a specific technical problem - limitations in the database's ability to handle requests - that's directly impacting service availability. Options 1 and 2 are broader concepts within DevOps; option 3 incorrectly identifies the SLA as the root cause.

questions.q: During a code review for the new API deployment, Alex (DevOps) comments on a PR: 'The current error rate is exceeding our target. We need to ensure proper circuit breaker implementation to prevent cascading failures.' Considering Alex's comment, which of the following best describes his concern? A : He's worried about the overall system throughput and suggests optimizing database queries. B : He's concerned with potential overload on a single service, leading to instability, and is advocating for proactive fault tolerance mechanisms. C : He's focused solely on the application code itself, suggesting a thorough review of the business logic. D : He's questioning the accuracy of the monitoring dashboards and recommends adjusting alert thresholds.
options: He's worried about the overall system throughput and suggests optimizing database queries.
He's concerned with potential overload on a single service, leading to instability, and is advocating for proactive fault tolerance mechanisms.
He's focused solely on the application code itself, suggesting a thorough review of the business logic.
He's questioning the accuracy of the monitoring dashboards and recommends adjusting alert thresholds.
questions.explanation: Alex's comment highlights a critical aspect of SRE - preventing cascading failures. A circuit breaker pattern is designed to temporarily halt requests to a failing service, isolating it from the rest of the system and preventing overload. Option A is incorrect because circuit breakers address *fault tolerance*, not just throughput; options C and D are irrelevant to the core issue of potential systemic instability caused by a single point of failure. This reflects a key SRE principle: anticipating and mitigating failures proactively.

questions.q: During a PR review for the deployment of a new payment processing microservice, Liam (DevOps) notes: 'The recent spike in error rates coincides with increased transaction volume. We're seeing a significant increase in 5xx errors and a corresponding rise in latency - impacting our user experience.' Considering this context, which option best describes Liam's primary concern?
options: A: He is primarily concerned with the accuracy of the monitoring tools and suggests investigating potential data corruption issues.
B: He's focused on optimizing the application code to handle higher transaction loads, suggesting a refactoring approach.
C: He's worried about the system's ability to handle peak demand and is advocating for implementing robust scaling strategies to prevent service degradation.
D: He believes the current error rate threshold is too sensitive and recommends adjusting it to better reflect normal operational fluctuations.
questions.explanation: Liam's comment highlights a correlation between increased load and system instability, indicating an issue with scalability or resource constraints. Option C accurately reflects his concern - he's recognizing the need for proactive measures to ensure the system can handle peak demand without performance degradation. The other options misinterpret Liam's focus; data corruption (A), code optimization (B) and adjusting thresholds (D) are secondary concerns in this scenario.

exercises.title: Expand the Abbreviation
exercises.subtitle: 12 exercises - match the abbreviation to its full form and read the usage note. API, SSH, ORM, CDN, TLS, CORS, JWT, CI/CD, DNS, SLA, HTTP, YAML.

questions.q: What does API stand for?
options: Application Programming Interface
Application Protocol Integration
Automated Processing Index
Advanced Programming Instance
questions.explanation: Application Programming Interface - a set of rules and contracts that allow different software applications to communicate with each other. You may see it in: "We expose a REST API", "the third-party API returns JSON", "rate-limiting on the public API".

questions.q: What does SSH stand for?
options: System Security Host
Secure Socket Handler
Secure Shell Host
Secure Shell
questions.explanation: Secure Shell - a cryptographic network protocol for operating network services securely over an unsecured network. Most commonly used for remote server login: "SSH into the server", "add your SSH key to authorized_keys".

questions.q: What does ORM stand for?
options: Object Relational Mapping
Open Runtime Module
Object Reference Model
Optimised Resource Manager
questions.explanation: Object-Relational Mapping - a technique that lets you interact with a database using object-oriented code instead of raw SQL. Examples include SQLAlchemy (Python), Hibernate (Java), ActiveRecord (Ruby), Prisma (Node.js). "We use an ORM to avoid writing raw queries."

questions.q: What does CDN stand for?
options: Central Distribution Network
Cached Data Node
Cloud Data Network
Content Delivery Network
questions.explanation: Content Delivery Network - a geographically distributed group of servers that work together to provide fast delivery of internet content. "We serve static assets through a CDN", "CDN edge caches the images closest to the user", "cache invalidation on the CDN after each deploy".

questions.q: What does TLS stand for?
options: Transfer Link System
Transport Layer Security
Terminal Layer Signal
Trusted Login Service
questions.explanation: Transport Layer Security - a cryptographic protocol that provides end-to-end security for communications over a network. Successor to SSL. "Enforce TLS 1.2 minimum", "TLS termination at the load balancer", "the TLS certificate expired".

questions.q: What does CORS stand for?
options: Central Object Routing System
Cross-Origin Resource Sharing
Cached Origin Response Set
Cross-Origin Request Service
questions.explanation: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing - a browser mechanism that allows or restricts web applications running at one origin to make requests to a different origin. "CORS headers are missing", "configure CORS to allow our frontend domain", "the CORS preflight request fails".

questions.q: What does JWT stand for?
options: JSON Web Token
JSON Web Transfer
JavaScript Web Token
Java Web Tunnel
questions.explanation: JSON Web Token - a compact, URL-safe means of representing claims to be transferred between two parties. Pronounced "jot" (not J-W-T). "Sign the JWT with the private key", "check the JWT expiry time", "never store sensitive data in the JWT payload - it is base64-encoded, not encrypted".

questions.q: What does CI/CD stand for?
options: Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment
Code Integration / Code Delivery
Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery
Both A and C are correct
questions.explanation: Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery OR Deployment - CI/CD is a combined term. questions.q: What does DNS stand for?

Distributed Name Server
Domain Name System

questions.q: What does SLA stand for?

Service Level Agreement
Service Layer Architecture
System Level Agreement

High Transfer Protocol
Hyperlink Text Transport Protocol
HyperText Transfer Protocol

questions.q: What does YAML stand for?

Yet Another Markup Language
Your Application Manifest Loader
Yet Another Mapping Language

'Cold cache' describes when the application server hasn't recently accessed or refreshed cached data, resulting in slower retrieval times. Optimizing the SQL might help *eventually*, but addressing the cold cache is more critical for immediate improvement.
Cold cache refers solely to server-side caching strategies; optimizing the SQL query will automatically resolve the latency.
The term 'cold cache' is simply jargon used by senior developers and doesn't have a specific technical meaning; we should just focus on improving the SQL query.
questions.explanation: This question tests understanding of a common performance issue terminology. The default size of the thread pool likely isn't sufficient to cope with peak loads, causing this issue; scaling it would provide more capacity.

Dynamic Key Infrastructure Management
Distributed Key Identity Module

Distributed Mail Access and Relay Control
Dynamic Message Authentication and Routing Configuration
Data Management and Routing Compliance

questions.q: The security team says: 'Service-to-service calls must use mTLS.' What does mTLS stand for?
options: Multi-tenant Transport Layer Security
Mutual Transport Layer Security
Managed Token Layer System
Modular TLS

questions.q: The backend developer explains: 'We issue a JWT after login and the client sends it in every request.' What is JWT?

JSON Web Token
JavaScript Workflow Template
Joint Web Transfer

questions.q: PR Description: "Fix: Implement rate limiting on the API endpoint to mitigate potential DDoS attacks. Using a combination of Redis for caching and an algorithmic rate limiter."
options: throttling - applying limits to requests based on user or source.
authentication - verifying the identity of users accessing the API.
authorization - determining what actions a user is permitted to perform.
encryption - converting data into an unreadable format to protect confidentiality.
questions.explanation: The PR description refers to 'rate limiting', which is the correct term. Rate limiting involves setting restrictions on the number of requests that can be made within a specific timeframe. While authentication and authorization are related concepts in security, they aren't directly described here; encryption protects data *in transit* or *at rest*, not the rate of API calls. Understanding this terminology is crucial for discussing API security best practices during code reviews.

questions.q: PR Description: "Implement OAuth 2.0 for third-party API access."
options: authorization code - a secure method for granting temporary access to resources.
refresh token - used to obtain new access tokens without requiring user interaction.
access token - represents the authorization granted by the resource server and is short-lived.
identity token - contains claims about the authenticated user, often used in conjunction with an access token.
questions.explanation: OAuth 2.0 relies on tokens to manage access permissions. An access token grants temporary access, while a refresh token allows you to obtain new ones without re-authenticating the user. Understanding these distinctions is crucial for designing secure API integrations. The PR describes using OAuth 2.0, therefore the refresh token is the relevant term.

questions.q: Sarah : 'I'm seeing a lot of 503 errors on the user registration endpoint. I think we need to implement Idempotency Keys.' What does an Idempotency Key primarily address in a distributed system?
options: A: A cryptographic signature ensuring data integrity during transmission.
B: A unique identifier used to prevent duplicate requests from having unintended consequences, particularly when retried due to network issues or client errors.
C: A mechanism for automatically scaling backend servers based on request volume.
D: The process of encrypting sensitive user data before storing it in the database.
questions.explanation: Idempotency Keys are crucial for handling unreliable networks and retries. They ensure that a single request is processed only once, even if sent multiple times due to temporary failures - preventing unintended side effects like duplicate account creation or incorrect data updates. Option A describes digital signatures; option C concerns auto-scaling; and option D refers to encryption.

C: An automated process for deploying code changes to various environments - development, staging, production.
D: A centralized logging service that aggregates logs from all our applications into a single location.
questions.explanation: The question highlights a common issue with API access and asks about IAM roles. IAM (Identity and Access Management) is fundamentally about controlling who can do what within your system. It provides a way to define granular permissions based on user identities and attributes, granting only the necessary access to resources - in this case, profile updates - preventing unauthorized actions. Options A, C, and D describe entirely different security or operational concepts.

questions.q: John : 'I'm investigating a spike in failed API calls. The logs show many clients are sending the same request multiple times - it seems like we might need to implement retry logic with exponential backoff.' What does 'exponential backoff' refer to within this context?
options: A: A technique for automatically increasing the timeout value on each failed API call, gradually extending the waiting period.
B: A strategy where the system attempts a request repeatedly, decreasing the delay between retries after each failure.
C: A method of encrypting sensitive data within the API request payload to prevent unauthorized access.
D: A process used to manually debug slow API calls by stepping through the code line by line.
questions.explanation: Exponential backoff is a key technique for handling transient failures in distributed systems. It involves increasing the delay between retry attempts after each failure, starting with a short delay and doubling it with each subsequent attempt - this prevents overwhelming the system during temporary outages. Option A is incorrect because timeout values are typically configured statically, not dynamically adjusted based on failure rates. Options C and D describe entirely different approaches to security and debugging.

questions.q: How is "SQL" most commonly pronounced in English-speaking tech teams?
options: "sequel"
"sql" (rhymes with "pull")
"S-Q-L" (three letters separately)
"squeal"
questions.explanation: "sequel" - SQL was originally called SEQUEL (Structured English Query Language) before being shortened to SQL. Most English-speaking developers say "sequel". You will occasionally hear "S-Q-L" (some database administrators and formal documentation prefer this). Both are understood, but "sequel" is the dominant pronunciation in day-to-day conversation. Usage: "Let me write a sequel query", "the sequel database", "sequel server" (Microsoft SQL Server).

questions.q: How is "NGINX" correctly pronounced?
options: "N-G-I-N-X" (spelled out)
"engine-x"
"en-GINKS"
"en-ginx" (rhymes with links)
questions.explanation: "engine-x" - NGINX is pronounced "engine-x". This comes from the original Russian pronunciation (Nginx was created by Igor Sysoev). The logo reinforces this with the stylised N. You will almost never hear a native speaker say "N-G-I-N-X" in conversation. Usage: "The engine-x config lives in /etc/nginx/", "proxy through engine-x with SSL termination".

questions.q: How is "GIF" most commonly pronounced?
options: "gif" (hard g, rhymes with "gift")
"G-I-F" (spelled out)
"jiff" (soft g, rhymes with "if")
Both are widely accepted
questions.explanation: Both are widely accepted - This is genuinely contested. Steve Wilhite, GIF's creator, insisted on "jiff" (soft g). Many developers use "gif" (hard g, like "gift"). Both are immediately understood. The creator's preference is "jiff" but the hard-g pronunciation is equally common and not wrong. You will not be corrected for either. Just stay consistent within a conversation.

questions.q: How is "JWT" typically pronounced in conversation?
options: "J-W-T" (three letters separately)
"jah-wt"
"jwt" (as one syllable)
"jot" (rhymes with "hot")
questions.explanation: "jot" - JWT (JSON Web Token) is informally pronounced "jot" by most developers. This is the official preferred pronunciation according to the JWT specification (RFC 7519). In formal contexts you may spell it out letter by letter (J-W-T), but in daily conversation "jot" is standard. "I signed the jot with the private key", "check the jot expiry", "the jot payload is base64-encoded".

questions.q: How is "IPv6" pronounced?
options: "I-P-version-six"
"I-P-v-six"
"IPsix"
Both A and B are correct and used interchangeably
questions.explanation: Both "I-P-version-six" and "I-P-v-six" are correct - you will hear both in conversation. "IPv6" is typically read as "I-P-v-six" in fast speech and "I-P-version-six" in formal or explanatory contexts. "Migrate to I-P-v-six addressing" and "the server doesn't support I-P-version-six yet" are both natural. Note: IPv4 follows the same pattern - "I-P-v-four" or "I-P-version-four".

options: "LY-nux" (long I, rhymes with "minus")
"LIN-ux" (short I, rhymes with "in")
"LIN-oox"
Both A and B are widely accepted
questions.explanation: Both "LY-nux" (American style) and "LIN-ux" are widely used - Linus Torvalds himself pronounces it "LIN-us" (short I), consistent with his Finnish name Linus. However, "LY-nux" (long I) is also very common in American English. In practice you will hear both and neither is wrong. For reference, Linus's recorded pronunciation is at kernel.org. Linux distributions like "Linus-inspired Unix" make the short-I reading logical.

British and Australian developers tend to say "char" (rhymes with "bar"/"car"). American developers often say "char" rhyming with "care" or "air". "kyoo-ber-NET-ees"
"koo-BER-neh-tees"
"KOO-ber-neh-tis"
